BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The seasonably cool and unsettled pattern will continue through the long-term period. With zonal flow aloft offering multiple opportunity for shortwave passages.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry with gradually warming temps through Monday morning. Frost and/or freezing temps in agricultural valleys this morning.
- Light rain and mountain snow Monday afternoon through Tuesday morning.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Another chilly morning is in store today with minimum temperatures of 15-25 degrees in E-Oregon and higher SW-Idaho basins, and then mid-20s to mid-30s elsewhere. Southwesterly flow aloft today will bring increasing high clouds and warmer temperatures; with high temps climbing to around 5 degrees above normal (generally mid 60s in lower elevations and mid 50s in mountain valleys).

Come Monday into Tuesday a closed upper level low will move inland across the Northern Rockies. Ahead of this system, breezy west- southwest winds will set in Monday afternoon, with gusts to 20-30 mph, strongest south and west of the Snake River Plain. These winds will transition to be west-northwest following a west to east moving cold front Monday afternoon into Monday night. While this system is not as wet as the previous one, showers will increase Monday afternoon into Monday night, especially over the Central Idaho Mountains. Over the course of Monday and Tuesday, precipitation amounts of 0.15-0.35 inches are forecast for the Central Idaho Mountains, with elsewhere remaining under 0.15 inches. While surface temperatures will be cool (highs across lower elevations a few degrees cooler than Monday, and higher terrain 5-10 degrees cooler), cooling aloft will support weak instability across higher terrain; this instability will lead to a slight chance of thunderstorms over terrain come Monday afternoon. Lowering snow levels will allow for a dusting to a few inches of snow for elevations above 6kft MSL.

Isolated to scattered showers will continue across higher terrain north through Tuesday. Following the cold frontal passage, high temperatures on Tuesday will be back near normal if not a few degrees below, with breezy conditions tapering off.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The seasonably cool and unsettled pattern will continue through the long-term period. With zonal flow aloft offering multiple opportunity for shortwave passages. The next notable system will approach the area late this week, although uncertainty remains on exact location, magnitude, and timing. Precipitation chances will increase Late Thursday into Friday to 20-60% (highest north and east of the Snake River Plain) as the low digs down into the northwest (which there is good ensemble agreement on). The question becomes whether or not the low aloft rejoins the main flow or breaks off to the south. The former of the two would keep showers over our area through Sunday, with the later offering a brief period of drying come late Saturday before bringing more widespread precipitation Sunday. With that uncertainty, elevated precipitation chances will be carried through Sunday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Heading towards the end of the work week, a negtaively-tilted ridge will begin to amplify, with the ridge axis located mainly to the east of our area, placing us under southwesterly flow.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cooler this weekend with temperatures around 5 to 10 degrees below normal.
- Widespread rain and mountain snowfall expected Sunday and Monday as a central Pacific system lifts northeast across the region.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday into Wednesday, but the next Pacific system will be approaching from the Pacific Northwest by the middle of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A pretty quiet afternoon ahead as stable conditions engulf the region behind a cold front that swept across CWA earlier today. This will keep high temperatures this afternoon slightly cooler than average, with highs west of I-25 topping out around 50 degrees and lower to mid 50s east of the corridor. Blustery northerly winds behind the front will taper off through the afternoon hours. Switching gears a bit and taking a look at the upper levels, initially we have a cut- off low over the Desert Southwest while we sit under a southwesterly flow regime with a ridge to our east across the Mississippi Valley. As we progress in the short term period, the cut off low will lift northeast and as it does so, the flow aloft over the CWA will become difluent, this combined with a plume of moisture in the southwest flow will support increased precipitation chances across the CWA this weekend. It will take a bit for us to see impacts here locally as a stable airmass over us will hold firm for most of today, so the impacts will not start until this evening as the atmosphere become saturated. But, before that, we may see returns on radar, with the dry layer at the lower levels of the atmosphere, any precipitation will struggle to hit the surface through at least the afternoon hours. As the atmosphere saturates, look for showers to become more widespread and persist throughout most of Sunday.

Lets take a closer look at Sunday, the low over the Southwest will continue to lift northeast closer to our CWA. Guidance indicates a surge of moisture ahead of this system, with ensemble members having PWATs above the 90th to 98th percentile. With adequate forcing with the aforementioned system, moderate rainfall looks to be a possibility. So, with ingredients in place, this looks like a scenario where up to 0.3" of rainfall, locally higher amounts, looks to be a possibility across the CWA, with lower amounts west of the Laramie Range. As the best dynamics sets up across the Nebraska Panhandle, many locations there have the best chances of seeing 1.0" of precipitation. To keep the forecast consistent, kept PoPs above 60 percent, mainly outside of Carbon County. Lower elevations should see all rain while the mountains will see sub advisory snowfall, with amounts on the order of 5.0" or less. Expect slightly cooler temperatures for Sunday as highs will only top out mid to upper 40s across the region as lows Sunday night tank to near freezing by Monday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: No major changes in the long term period, please see previous discussion...

The work week will begin unsettled as a weak, inverted lee trough will be located to our south and east over the Central High Plains. This feature is associated with a rather broad mid-level shortwave trough, placing much of the Nebraska Panhandle at the inflection point between a weak downstream ridge located over the Upper Midwest, resulting in upper-level ageostrophic divergence and the formation of a weak surface low to our east. The strongest forcing for ascent at this time looks to set up over the Nebraska Panhandle and points further east, bringing chances for precipitation primarily east of the I-25 corridor during the day on Monday. Ensembles at this time have trended down from previous runs, with ECMWF ensemble means having 0.15-0.2" of QPF for Cheyenne, with locations in the Panhandle seeing upwards of 0.5", which would certainly help out with our drought conditions. Ensemble guidance suggests PWAT at or above the 95th percentile relative to climatology (~0.7") in the Panhandle, so heavy rain will be a threat especially if we see any convective elements over the area despite the main instability axis progged to remain well to the south and east over Kansas and Central Nebraska.

In terms of precipitation type, temperatures at this time look to be too warm for any snow (generally below 8000-9000 feet), as LREF guidance keeps 25th percentile minimum temperatures mainly in the mid to upper 30s east of the I-25 corridor, with low to mid-30s Monday morning for locations west of the Laramie Range. Places like Rawlins and Laramie will be away from the bulk of the forcing for ascent at this time, so will likely stay dry despite seeing slightly cooler temperatures. A weak cold front is progged to move through SE Wyoming and the NE Panhandle sometime late Monday into early Tuesday, which will result in slightly cooler overnight lows Tuesday morning, with locations west of I-25 waking up to temperatures at or slightly below freezing, and mid to upper 30s to the east. The shortwave trough ejects off to the north and east during the day Tuesday, placing us under a SW flow regime on the southern periphery of a rather amplified negatively-tilted shortwave trough lifting over Idaho and the Northern Great Basin. The strongest forcing for ascent looks to remain well to our north over Northern Wyoming and the Dakotas, so conditions for us look to remain mostly dry, with the exception of the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges which may manage to pick up some light snowfall, though ensemble guidance keeps totals under 1-2" and confined to the higher peaks. High temperatures on Tuesday are expected to be at or slightly above climatology with highs in the low 60s east of the Laramie Range, and low 50s to the west.

Wednesday, anticyclonic wave breaking over Northern British Columbia will serve to strengthen the geopotential height gradient associated with a closed low located off the coast of the Pacific Northwest. This, combined with an additional secondary shortwave trough located off the Oregon coast will serve to increase southwesterly 700-500 mb flow up to 50-60 knots, introducing the possibility for a high wind event, primarily for our wind-prone areas of Arlington and Bordeaux (tis' the season!). Model cross-sections along the I-80 corridor show mountain wave signatures that are reflective in the omega fields, however a mountain-top stable layer is lacking, which may be a limiting factor for a more high-end and widespread high wind event. As it stands, in-house random forecast guidance has around 40% probabilities of Arlington experiencing high wind conditions Wednesday morning, with Bordeaux at around 20%, so while it may be gusty, stay tuned for potential high wind highlights as we get closer to this timeframe. Given gusty, downsloping conditions, high temperatures on Wednesday will continue to remain mild, with highs slightly above climatology in the low 60s east of the I-25 corridor, and 50s to the west.

Heading towards the end of the work week, a negtaively-tilted ridge will begin to amplify, with the ridge axis located mainly to the east of our area, placing us under southwesterly flow. As 500 mb height anomalies increase to +1-2 sigma relative to climatology, can expect dry conditions and a slight warming trend.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: This low finally moves east of the Divide by Monday morning, with much drier conditions expected through the day Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding is ongoing across portions of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado, and is expected to continue through Sunday morning.
- Rivers continue to run full, with a few cresting already and some expected to crest overnight tonight into early Sunday morning.
- Scattered showers and storms will be capable of producing moderate to heavy rainfall that could result in additional local flooding through Sunday.
- Mountain passes could see some light snow on roadways tonight, and again Sunday night into Monday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The slow moving area of low pressure that has kept the last several days cool and wet remains in place around the Four Corners, pumping more tropical moisture into the region. Rain showers, and a few thunderstorms, will continue to move from south to north through eastern Utah and western Colorado through the night tonight. At the higher elevations, light snowfall will be possible above 9-10k feet. Little in the way of accumulations are expected, but it could lead to slippery commutes over the southern mountain passes Sunday morning. While rain rates remain on the lower side, these showers will contribute more runoff into the already waterlogged rivers and streams. While a number of rivers have already crested and are on their way down, a few rivers, particularly the San Juan River through the Four Corners and Southeast Utah, continue to rise. A Flood Watch, and a number of Flood Warnings, remain in place through Sunday afternoon to capture the expected crests in the next 6-12 hours.

Drier air tries to push in from the southwest during the day tomorrow as the low finally starts to lift northeast. This will bring a break from showers before the cold frontal passage reinvigorates showers and storms during the afternoon. These storms will be capable of producing brief heavy rain, frequent lightning, small hail, and gusty winds. Colder air in the wake of the front and lingering moisture will allow for light mountain rain and snow showers to linger Sunday night into Monday. Again, little snow accumulation is expected, but passes could once again be slippery Monday morning, especially along the Central and Northern Divide.

This low finally moves east of the Divide by Monday morning, with much drier conditions expected through the day Monday. A quick moving clipper will just brush our northern border Monday night into Tuesday, with the potential for some light rain and snow showers over the higher terrain of the eastern Uintas and Northern Colorado Divide. Behind this clipper, zonal flow takes control, bringing mostly quiet conditions and gradually warming temperatures through the back half of the work week. Highs start out 5-10 degrees below normal Sunday through Tuesday, climbing to near-normal by the Wednesday-Thursday time period. By Friday, flow aloft shifts to a moister southwesterly direction in response to a low deepening off the West Coast, bringing increased cloud cover and a slight cooldown. Model agreement is poor beyond this point, but there are indications that we could see a return to cooler and unsettled conditions by next weekend.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: The next concern will be next weekend. The strong EL NINO over the Pacific is likely to continue to roar as an impressive subtropical jet si forecast to develop and push another round of moisture towards the southwest CONUS.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Heavy rain likely to occur over parts of the southeast plains this afternoon into tonight.
- Low lying agricultural flooding in the western side of the San Luis Valley likely for the next day or two.
- Another impactful storm possible next weekend (hopefully more snow then rain).

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The main concern in the short term will be a slow moving front across the plains. This system. combined with plenty of high quality low level moisture and a stout disturbance moving over the state will allow for heavy rain to occur across parts of the plains, mainly south and east of a line from Haswell to Fowler to Trinidad. 1 to 2 inches, with local 3 inch amounts, of rain will be likely in this region between this afternoon and Sunday evening.
In addition to the heavy rain, some of the storm that occur along this boundary may be on the strong side, with marginal severe weather possible.

Another area of lesser concern this afternoon and evening is over the San Juans and San Luis Valley. Although this area will receive another 0.25 to 0.75 inches (with local higher amounts), the brunt of it above ~9000 fee will be in the form of snow (and thus no run- off) as temperatures over the higher terrain have cooled off to around freezing. In addition, the heavy rainfall rates that occurred with the initial first short wave are not expected due to the much cooler temperatures. Nonetheless, any rain over saturated soils is not good, but the impacts of this new rainfall should be minor (modest rises on area streams/rivers).

By tomorrow morning, showers will still be lingering over the mtns, with steady rain likely still ongoing across the far eastern counties on the plains. This heavier rain over the far southeastern plains may pick up again during the afternoon as another jet streak moves through the longwave trough.

As for snowfall, I wouldn't be too surprised at the very top of the mtns will get some decent 4 to locally 8 inch amounts, especially over the La Garitas, the central mtns and the northern Sangre De Cristo mtns. The tops of Pikes Peak may see a few inches.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: For Monday onward into the end of the week, it should primarily be dry with cooler temperatures over the region (60s/L70s plains).

The next concern will be next weekend. The strong EL NINO over the Pacific is likely to continue to roar as an impressive subtropical jet si forecast to develop and push another round of moisture towards the southwest CONUS. This jet, combined with another impressive Pacific trough should bring another round of impactful precip to the region. This scenarios reflected in both the deterministic and statistical guidance products (see any of the high elevation sites on the NBM-1D viewer for next weekend). The good news is this next weather system should be cooler and more of the precip over our higher elevations should be snow. Of course the details still need to be worked out, but next weekend looks like another active period for the region. \/Hodanish

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: A near zonal flow pattern is expected to develop on Tuesday before southwesterly flow develops on Wednesday as a weakening and relatively benign trough grazes northern Utah. Thereafter, another storm system will reach the PacNW coast by Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered showers with embedded thunderstorms will continue through Sunday across eastern Utah which will keep a low threat for flash flooding given the saturated soils.
- Pattern remains unsettled with a quick moving cold front Monday night followed by a more substantial storm by the end of the week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The large-scale pattern this evening consists of a closed low centered over northwest Arizona while upstream, another closed low is located off the southern BritCol coast. The low over Arizona resulted in some isolated to scattered showers over portions of southern and eastern Utah earlier today, with much of this having already decreased this evening. However, a vort lobe embedded within the low will rotate into southeast Utah tonight. This is expected to bring an increasing threat of showers with a few embedded thunderstorms back to southern and eastern Utah, mainly after midnight. As the rest of the upper low lifts through the Four Corners area through the day Sunday, expect generally scattered showers and thunderstorms to continue over roughly the spine of Utah and points east. Can not rule out an isolated flash flood with stronger showers moving over a sensitive basin.

A relative lull in precipitation is expected for Monday as a transient shortwave ridge crosses the area. Temperatures on Monday will trend warmer under the ridge, with northern Utah returning closer to normal while southern Utah will remain below normal.

Meanwhile, the closed low over the BritCol coast will move inland across the PacNW Sunday night into Monday before grazing northern Utah Monday night as a fast-moving shortwave trough. This trough will push a relatively shallow cold front into northern Utah Monday night. This will drop temperatures across northern Utah to generally 4-8 degrees below normal for Tuesday. Generally light precipitation is expected near the cold front, though amounts will depend in part on the strength of the cold front, of which subtle changes could make a noticeable difference. The latest deterministic GFS and NAM are leaning towards a weaker front with lower QPF compared to the EC. The 19z NBM has 25th-75th percentile values of around 0.15-0.6 in the northern Wasatch Mountains and Bear River Range (highest along the Idaho border), and from less than 0.05-0.4 inches in the adjacent valleys. Snow levels look to fall to between 6-7kft, so light snow accumulations can be expected in the mountains.

A near zonal flow pattern is expected to develop on Tuesday before southwesterly flow develops on Wednesday as a weakening and relatively benign trough grazes northern Utah. Thereafter, another storm system will reach the PacNW coast by Thursday. This will tap into some moisture and bring potentially widespread precipitation back to the area as early as Friday and continuing through the weekend. However, the details on how this storm system will evolve (whether it splits, and how quickly it moves through the area, etc) are still pending better model agreement.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
